pr_title: Fix parsing of trailing zeros: TryParseNumber
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/46827

We're currently not throwing away the trailing zeros from the fractional part of a number while parsing. This leads us to erroneously round a floating point number sometimes. This PR fixes that. I've also updated the CheckConsistency method to detect trailing zeros.

Alright, the bug occurs because of this line:


issue_context.body:
<!--This is just a template - feel free to delete any and all of it and replace as appropriate.-->

### Description
Code to reproduce:
```csharp
using System;

class Program {
    public static void Main(string[] args) {
        Console.WriteLine("{0:R}", double.Parse("9007199254740997"));
        Console.WriteLine("{0:R}", double.Parse("900719925474099.7e+1"));
        Console.WriteLine("{0:R}", double.Parse("9007199254740997.0"));
        Console.WriteLine("{0:R}", double.Parse("90071992547409970e-1"));
    }
}
```

Actual output:
```
9007199254740996
9007199254740996
9007199254740998
9007199254740998
```
Expected: All four outputs should be the same. (9007199254740996 if rounding to even)
### Configuration

* Which version of .NET is the code running on? .NET 5
* What OS and version, and what distro if applicable? Windows 10
* What is the architecture (x64, x86, ARM, ARM64)? x64
* Do you know whether it is specific to that configuration? No

Looks like a bug. I'll investigate this as I work on https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/46874 next week!

Yup, reproduced it locally. Will look into this further this week.


This happens because of rounding due to the call [here](https://source.dot.net/#System.Private.CoreLib/Number.NumberToFloatingPointBits.cs,217). The `.0` is (correctly) interpreted as having a fractional part (=> HasZeroTail is `false`) that results in blind rounding. I'm not sure what the fix should be yet. Investigating...

Meanwhile, how did you find this bug?

review_comments: nit: It would be nice if the cases that returned `9007199254740996.0` were side by side with these ones; just to make it easier to spot check the difference between round down and round up
Done

It would probably be good to add explicit tests for just cases like `50050` and other scenarios that are integers with trailing zeros but no fractional part specified, to help ensure they don't regress.

You got other examples? AFAICT I've covered all the interesting cases?

``` 
9007199254740997.0
5.005
5.050
5005.0
50050.0
5005
050050
0.000
0.005
0.0500
```

We know there are bugs in the case where there there are trailing fractional zeros.

I was wanting at least one test covering trailing integral zeros, such as `"50050"` (in contrast to `"50050.0"`).
Do any of these cases suggest interseting missing test cases in SingleTests.cs or in DecimalTests.cs?
It would probably be good to ensure they are mirrored across the floating-point types (decimal, float, double, and half) to ensure they all have consistent coverage.

> Do any of these cases suggest interseting missing test cases in SingleTests.cs or in DecimalTests.cs?

I don't think so. The test cases here test the `TryParseNumber` method. All the other floating point types call `TryParseNumber`, so we should in theory be fine testing just 1 type. I'll update the test cases for all the types though, just in case

The main difference ends up being in edge case handling.

For example, `double` limits its buffer size to 768 digits, while `single` limits it to 113 digits, and only 20 for half.

It would probably be to validate some number that is, for example, that many digits + a non-zero digit to ensure it is handled correctly.

Imagine, for example, `0.500....0001` which is distinct from `0.500....0000`
(I'm not sure if the above case would actually be impacted by the rounding; just giving an example of where we may want to find and validate such a case)
Alright I fixed a bug in my changes around rounding when the last digit was == maxDigitCount and last digit > maxDigitCount. I've added some unit tests to cover it. This PR should be good now.
So in this situation, we are maintaining the trailing zeros in the buffer? Won't that conflict with the consistency check?
It should've. It probably didn't because of the way I was comparing `byte` and `0`. Fixed now.
I'm not familiar with cbor. Do we know why this changed in size?

Nor am I. I just figured that we are parsing correctly now and returning `1`. So I looked at the test case 2 lines above for `1` and copied that. I can go back and see what value we're returning without the bug fix, but I'm pretty sure it is wrong somehow and this PR is fixing it.

The number of hex digits implies it was over the length 32-bits, but it also looks like there is some general encoding (compression?) here so it's unclear whether the change is actually correct (I would guess it is though).

The original CBOR encodes `1000e-3`, while the new one is `1e0`, so I presume this is in line with the intended change in the parser.
